how_it_works: Each idea is checked in the same loop. The learner explains it in their own words; the model labels the explanation own, recited, wrong or unclear and quotes the sentence it means. Then case A, a new situation with one short answer written in advance, which code checks against accept and reject. If case A is right and the explanation was their own reasoning, that's 1 point. Otherwise the model asks one follow-up about the quoted sentence, then case B, a different situation chosen so the common wrong idea gives the wrong answer. Practice uses the practice cases and is never scored. The Real-world test uses the real_world cases and decides the score on the map.

ideas.idea: Why start from one real person's struggle?
ideas.explain: Why should an app idea start from watching one real person struggle, instead of a big idea like 'AI for productivity'?
ideas.simpler: What can you check with one real person that you can't check with a big idea?
ideas.understanding: With a real person and a real task you can do the job by hand, see what they actually need, and check whether your output helped them. A big idea gives you nothing to check against.
ideas.misconception: A bigger idea is better because more people could use it.
ideas.follow_up_seed: With 'AI for productivity', how would you know on day one whether your app helped anyone?

practice.scenario: Aarav spends 90 minutes every Friday writing a status report. Is that an observation or a big idea?

real_world.answer: a real person with a real task

ideas.idea: Why does a hypothesis need a number?
ideas.explain: Why does a hypothesis need a number that could prove you wrong?
ideas.simpler: If nothing could prove your idea wrong, how would you ever know it failed?
ideas.understanding: A number sets the bar before you start, so you can see clearly whether you hit it and learn something either way. Without one, any result can be called a success.
ideas.misconception: A hypothesis just needs to sound confident and positive.
ideas.follow_up_seed: Your app 'helps learners'. Ten people try it and three seem happier. Did it pass or fail? How would you decide?

practice.scenario: Which one can fail: 'Our app helps analysts' or '6 of 10 analysts build one automation in 2 weeks'?

real_world.scenario: A gym says, 'Members will love our new app.' After a month, 4 of 10 members open it weekly. Did the claim pass or fail?
A cafe's test: 'At least 30 of 100 customers will order the new coffee.' 22 order it. Pass or fail?

ideas.source: Lecture 8 notes (the 6 of 10 bet); Aarav Reference Document, Discovery Document tab

ideas.idea: Why write the ideal answer first?
ideas.explain: Why write the ideal answer for a test input before you see what the AI says?
ideas.simpler: If you read the AI's answer first, what might happen to your idea of a good answer?
ideas.understanding: Written first, the ideal answer is a fixed bar. Written after, you tend to accept whatever the AI said, so you can't catch it being wrong.
ideas.misconception: The AI's answer is the best guide to what a good answer looks like.
ideas.follow_up_seed: The AI gives a confident but wrong plan, and you write your ideal answer after reading it. What's likely to end up in your ideal answer?

practice.scenario: You write the ideal plan for Aarav's Friday report, then test the AI against it. What is that input and ideal answer together called?

real_world.scenario: A teacher marks an exam. Should she write the answer key before or after reading the students' answers?
A food critic decides what 'great biryani' means only after tasting one restaurant's biryani. Can she now judge that restaurant fairly?

ideas.idea: Why isn't 'it runs' a verifier?
ideas.explain: Why isn't 'the code runs' or 'it looks good' enough to say your AI app works?
ideas.simpler: Who decides whether the output helped: the code, or the person using it?
ideas.understanding: Code can run and still give useless output, and 'looks good' changes with mood. A verifier is a written condition about whether the output helps the user, checked the same way every time.
ideas.misconception: If there are no errors, the app works.
ideas.follow_up_seed: Aarav can't read Python. What would you write down as the test his plan must pass?

practice.scenario: The app runs with no errors and returns a plan full of Python code. Aarav can't read Python. Did the app work for Aarav?

real_world.scenario: A delivery app's route finder never crashes, but sends riders down a closed road every day. Does the route finder work?
A translation app gives perfect grammar but the wrong meaning. What should its test check: the grammar or the meaning?

ideas.idea: Search, form or chat?
ideas.explain: How do you decide whether your app needs a search box, a form or a chat?
ideas.simpler: Do you already know exactly what the user will type?
ideas.understanding: Search finds something that already exists. A form fits when the inputs are known and fixed. A chat fits when the input is open-ended and needs back-and-forth.
ideas.misconception: Chat is always best because it's the most flexible.
ideas.follow_up_seed: Aarav's leave request always needs a start date, an end date and a reason. What would a chat add that three boxes don't?

practice.scenario: Aarav wants to find last month's diagnosis that mentioned Jira. Search, form or chat?
Every leave request needs a start date, an end date and a reason, nothing else. Search, form or chat?

real_world.scenario: You want to find a song you heard yesterday by typing part of its name. Search, form or chat?
A credit card application needs name, PAN, income and address. A startup wants to turn it into a chat. Form or chat?

ideas.idea: Why do the job by hand first?
ideas.explain: Why do the whole job by hand for one real user before writing any code?
ideas.simpler: What do you learn by doing the job yourself that you can't learn by coding it?
ideas.understanding: Doing it by hand shows you the real process and what a good output looks like, cheaply, before code locks in your guesses. It also gives you real golden pairs.
ideas.misconception: Building the app first is faster; you learn by shipping code.
ideas.follow_up_seed: You code for three weeks, then Aarav says the plan isn't what he needed. What would one plan sent by WhatsApp have cost you instead?

practice.scenario: Before writing code, you write Aarav's plan yourself and send it on WhatsApp. What is this way of testing called?

real_world.answer: take and deliver orders by hand

ideas.idea: What does one API call carry?
ideas.explain: What does a request to Groq need to carry? Why can't it skip any of them?
ideas.simpler: If you posted a letter to a machine, what would you need to put on it?
ideas.understanding: An address (where it goes), an action (what to do), a key (who's asking) and a package (what's being sent). Each answers something the machine can't guess.
ideas.misconception: The address is enough; the machine works out the rest.
ideas.follow_up_seed: Two requests go to the same address. How does the machine know one wants to read and the other wants to delete?

practice.scenario: Your request reaches the right address but has no key. What does the machine ask you?

ideas.idea: Why can't the key live in the browser?
ideas.explain: Why can't the Groq key go in your page's code? What could someone do with it?
ideas.simpler: Your page is sent to everyone who visits. What does that mean for a key inside it?
ideas.understanding: The page reaches every visitor's machine, where anyone can read it. A key works for whoever holds it, so they could use it as you and spend your quota or money.
ideas.misconception: HTTPS, or hiding the key in the code, keeps it safe.
ideas.follow_up_seed: A stranger copies your key from the page. What could they do with it tomorrow, and who pays?

ideas.idea: Why is asking the AI a POST?
ideas.explain: Why is asking the AI a POST, but a Google search a GET?
ideas.simpler: Does the AI's answer exist before you ask?
ideas.understanding: GET reads something that already exists and changes nothing. The AI's reply is new each time (ask twice, get two replies), so it's a create: POST.
ideas.misconception: You're getting an answer back, so it should be a GET.
ideas.follow_up_seed: Ask the AI the same question twice. Do you get the same reply? What does that say about whether the reply already existed?

Aarav asks the AI for a new plan and waits to get it back. Which action?

ideas.idea: Why can PUT wipe what PATCH keeps?
ideas.explain: Why can PUT wipe out fields that PATCH leaves alone?
ideas.simpler: One replaces the whole thing, one changes just a part. Which is which?
ideas.understanding: PUT replaces the whole thing with what you send, so anything you leave out is gone. PATCH changes only the fields you send.
ideas.misconception: PUT and PATCH are the same: both just update.
ideas.follow_up_seed: You send PUT with only the title. What happens to the steps you didn't send?

practice.scenario: Workflow 7 has a title, a frequency and steps. You PATCH only the frequency. Are the steps still there?
Same workflow. This time you PUT only the frequency. Are the steps still there?

real_world.scenario: You change only your profile photo on Instagram. Should the app PATCH or PUT your profile?
An app sends PUT with just your new phone number. What happens to your name and address on the profile?

ideas.idea: Whose fault is it?
ideas.explain: A request fails. How does the first number of the status code tell you where to look?
ideas.simpler: If the code starts with 4, whose mistake is it? And if it starts with 5?
ideas.understanding: 4xx means something in your request is wrong, so fix what you sent. 5xx means the server failed, so look at the server and its logs.
ideas.misconception: Any error means their server is broken.
ideas.follow_up_seed: You get a 404 and decide to wait an hour for their server to recover. Will waiting fix it?

practice.scenario: You get a 404. Do you fix your request, or wait for their server?
Groq replies 401. Is Groq down?

real_world.scenario: At 10 am during Tatkal booking, IRCTC shows a 503. Your internet works fine. Whose problem is it?
A shopping app replies 400: 'invalid PIN code'. Is the shop's server broken?

ideas.idea: Why doesn't 200 mean you got what you wanted?
ideas.explain: Why can a request come back 200 OK and still not give you what you wanted?
ideas.simpler: Does 200 mean 'you got what you wanted', or 'your request was fine'?
ideas.understanding: 200 means the request was understood and handled. If you asked the wrong thing, or nothing exists yet, you get a correct but empty or unwanted answer.
ideas.misconception: 200 means success, so everything worked.
ideas.follow_up_seed: You ask for Aarav's plans before he has made any. The server replies 200. What's in the list?

practice.scenario: Aarav asks for his plans before creating any. The reply is 200 with an empty list. Is the server broken?

real_world.scenario: You search Swiggy for pizza at 3 am and get an empty list with a 200. Is the app broken?
Your bank's balance request comes back 200, but for your old, closed account. Did you get what you wanted?

ideas.idea: Why does a backend exist at all?
ideas.explain: Why does Aarav's app need a backend? Say what would go wrong without one.
ideas.simpler: What job does the backend do that the page can't?
ideas.understanding: Some work must run on a machine the user can't see into or change: holding the key, calling the AI, saving data. The page only asks.
ideas.misconception: A backend is only needed for heavy work.
recitation_markers: frontend is ui, backend is logic
ideas.follow_up_seed: If the page called Groq itself, with the key inside, who else could use that key?

practice.scenario: Aarav's page needs a plan from Groq. Which machine should send that request?
Aarav's app is tiny and does almost no work. What does it still need a backend to hide?

ideas.idea: Why test the AI differently from normal code?
ideas.explain: Why do you test the AI part of your app differently from normal code?
ideas.simpler: If you ask the AI the same thing twice, do you get the exact same words?
ideas.understanding: Normal code gives the same output for the same input, so you can check it exactly. The AI's words change each time, so you check it against a written condition, not an exact match.
ideas.misconception: The AI is a program, so it always gives the same answer.
ideas.follow_up_seed: You save Monday's AI reply and check that Tuesday's reply matches it word for word. What happens?

practice.scenario: Your add(2, 3) function returns 5. You run it again. What does it return?

ideas.idea: Why does the key go in an environment variable?
ideas.explain: Why does the key go in an environment variable instead of in your code?
ideas.simpler: Who can read your code once it's on GitHub or on a shared screen?
ideas.understanding: Code gets shared: GitHub, screenshots, reviews. An environment variable keeps the key outside the code, on the machine that runs it, so sharing the code doesn't share the key.
ideas.misconception: If the repo is private, a key in the code is fine.
ideas.follow_up_seed: You push code with the key typed into it to a public repo. Who has your key now?

ideas.idea: What changes when you switch AI provider?
ideas.explain: You call Groq with plain requests. If you switch to OpenAI, what changes and what stays the same?
ideas.simpler: Every machine needs an address, an action, a key and a package. Which of those change between companies?
ideas.understanding: The address, the key and the model name change. The shape stays the same: a POST with a key in the header and a JSON package.
ideas.misconception: Each AI company needs a completely different way of calling it.
ideas.follow_up_seed: Write the four parts of your Groq call. Which of them mention Groq?

practice.scenario: You switch from Groq to OpenAI. Does the action change from POST?
You switch from Groq to OpenAI. Name one thing you must change.
practice.answer: the address, the key or the model

A weather app switches to a new weather provider. Does it need to be rewritten from scratch?

ideas.idea: Why check every package that arrives?
ideas.explain: Why does your API check every incoming package before running any code?
ideas.simpler: What happens if your code expects text and someone sends a photo?
ideas.understanding: Your route is open to the whole internet, and people will send wrong or empty packages. Checking first turns them away with a clear error instead of letting your code crash.
ideas.misconception: Only your own page calls the API, so the input is always right.
ideas.follow_up_seed: Someone sends 'text' where your code expects 'workflow'. Without a check, what does your code do?

Someone skips a shopping site's page and sends its API a price of ₹1 for a phone. Who must catch it: the page or the server?

ideas.idea: Why does a localhost link only work for you?
ideas.explain: Why does http://127.0.0.1:8000 work on your laptop but not when you send it to Aarav?
ideas.simpler: Whose machine does 127.0.0.1 point to?
ideas.understanding: 127.0.0.1 means 'this machine'. On Aarav's laptop it points at his own laptop, where your app isn't running. Others need a deployed address on a machine everyone can reach.
ideas.misconception: The link is broken, or Aarav's internet is the problem.
ideas.follow_up_seed: When Aarav opens 127.0.0.1 on his laptop, which machine is his browser asking?

ideas.idea: Why does the app forget without storage?
ideas.explain: On Tuesday Aarav asks about Monday's plan, and the app has no idea. Why does it forget?
ideas.simpler: What does the app remember between two messages?
ideas.understanding: Every request starts from nothing. The AI only sees what this request carries, and nothing kept Monday's plan.
ideas.misconception: The AI remembers past chats by itself.
ideas.follow_up_seed: What did Tuesday's request actually contain? What was missing from it?

ideas.idea: How do you decide where a piece lives?
ideas.explain: How do you decide which machine a part of your app should live on?
ideas.simpler: Why does the AI model live on Groq's machine and not on Aarav's laptop?
ideas.understanding: Ask two things: does it fit (size and memory), and who may see or wipe it (privacy)? Too big or private goes to a machine you or someone else controls; small and harmless can live with the user.
ideas.misconception: Everything should just go on the server.
ideas.follow_up_seed: The model needs 65 GB of memory and Aarav's laptop has 8 GB. Where can it run?

ideas.idea: Why does the pointer sit on the many side?
ideas.explain: One conversation has many messages. Why does each message store conversation_id, and not the other way round?
ideas.simpler: Can one box in a table hold a list of many numbers?
ideas.understanding: A cell holds one value. Each message belongs to exactly one conversation, so each message can hold one pointer. A conversation can't fit many ids in one cell.
ideas.misconception: The newer table points to the older one.
recitation_markers: the foreign key goes on the many side
ideas.follow_up_seed: Conversation 7 has 3 messages. What would one message_ids cell on conversations have to hold?

practice.scenario: One user writes many workflows, and each workflow has one owner. Which table gets the pointer?
A team is created after its members joined. Each member is in one team, and a team has many members. Which table gets the pointer?

real_world.scenario: On IRCTC, one train has many bookings, and each booking is for one train. Which table holds train_number?
Swiggy creates a delivery batch after the orders were placed. One batch has many orders, and each order is in one batch. Which table gets batch_id?

ideas.idea: Why is history a row, not a cell?
ideas.explain: Why save each new plan as a new row, instead of changing the old one?
ideas.simpler: What happens to the old value when you change a cell?
ideas.understanding: Changing a cell overwrites the old value. New rows, each with a time, keep every version.
ideas.misconception: The database keeps old values by itself.
ideas.follow_up_seed: Workflow 7's plan cell now says plan B. Where is plan A?

ideas.idea: Why does a file break with many writers?
ideas.explain: memory.txt worked for one person. Why does it lose data when two people save at once?
ideas.simpler: Two people edit the same file and both press save. Whose changes stay?
ideas.understanding: Both read the whole file, add a line, and write the whole file back, so the second write wipes out the first.
ideas.misconception: Files break because they get too big.
ideas.follow_up_seed: Jagan and Vineet both read the file at 10:00, add a line each and write it back. Whose line survives?

ideas.idea: Why does the database check whose row it is?
ideas.explain: Why should the database itself check whose row it is, instead of trusting your server code to filter?
ideas.simpler: If your code forgets one 'only my rows' filter, who could see Aarav's rows?
ideas.understanding: Code can have bugs or be bypassed. A row level security rule in the database checks every query against the logged-in user, so even a mistaken or injected query only returns that user's own rows.
ideas.misconception: If the app has a login screen, the data is already safe.
